first.rationale:
The measured deficits are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing the funnel entry plausibly recovers both. Two independent inherited records (memory_86 on shortened onboarding, memory_31 on signup field reduction) point the same way, which is the strongest convergence available. I spend the single verification pull on memory_86 because it is the most load-bearing claim for the action I intend and the one whose framing is vaguest: 'lifting early product adoption' does not tell me whether the lift persisted past the first week, whether it held for the self-serve segment now under competitive pressure, or whether completion rose merely because steps were removed rather than because more accounts reached value. If the source record shows the effect was a short-horizon completion artifact, I would fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which targets the same funnel with a different mechanism.

I deliberately do not choose promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing. memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift but is silent on retention and on the quality of the accounts acquired; discount-led response to a price war risks importing exactly the price-sensitive, low-durability cohort that degrades long-term qualified revenue, and it invites margin matching we cannot sustain. That is the primary downstream value risk here. A secondary risk applies to my own choice: stripping signup and onboarding fields can reduce qualification data and routing quality, so lead quality and enterprise routing must be instrumented as guardrail metrics, not just completion rate.

Uncertainty I am not collapsing: all six memories predate the competitor launch, so the environment that produced them has shifted, and the current declines may be caused by competitive diversion rather than any funnel defect, in which case a funnel fix will underperform its historical effect size. memory_44 and memory_57 concern segments (enterprise, established customers) that do not address this quarter's deficits and are not credible one-week responses. Standard experiment scale with a clean holdout is appropriate: the evidence is convergent enough to justify more than a token test, but too dated to justify broad rollout without fresh measurement.

final.rationale:
The archive strengthens rather than merely restates memory_86: completion +13% is paired with time-to-value -2.1 days and 30-day retention +3%. That third figure is the one I was worried about. It rules out the failure mode where completion rises only because steps were deleted and accounts pass through without reaching value; accounts that finished the shorter flow were still present and engaged a month later. Combined with memory_31 arriving at a compatible conclusion by a different mechanism (signup field reduction rather than flow shortening), this is the best-supported direction available, and it targets both current deficits at once since onboarding sits upstream of activation.

I hold to rejecting promotional_pricing as the competitive response. memory_73 remains unverified and silent on retention, which is precisely the dimension memory_86 now has evidence on. Answering entry pricing with discounts risks acquiring a low-durability, price-elastic cohort and starting a margin contest we cannot win, which cuts directly against sustainable long-term qualified revenue. memory_44 and memory_57 address segments unrelated to this quarter's declines. activation_messaging (memory_91) stays the fallback if onboarding instrumentation shows no movement.

Residual uncertainty I am not collapsing. First, exp_86 predates the competitor launch, so its effect size was measured in an environment where price-sensitive SMBs were not being actively diverted; if the current declines are driven by competitive loss rather than funnel friction, the replication will underperform +13% even if the mechanism is sound. Second, the source record reports no sample size, segment breakdown, or confidence interval, so I treat +13% as directional rather than as a forecast. Third, the earlier risk stands on its own merits: removing fields can degrade qualification data and enterprise routing, and completion rate alone would hide that. Run at standard scale with a clean holdout, instrumenting lead quality, routing accuracy, and 30-day retention as guardrails alongside completion and activation, and preregister a rollback if guardrails move adversely. Evidence is strong enough for a real test, too dated to justify broad rollout unmeasured.
